title: Architecture & Data Contract
content:
The architecture is divided into a Data Lake path and a Serving path. The bridge between them is Lambda QMJ Loader: S3 creates new Parquet files, S3 sends an ObjectCreated event, and Lambda reads the file and writes items to DynamoDB.
Data Flow Data Lake path Sources → Backfill/Daily Ingestion → S3 Raw → Glue PySpark QMJ → S3 Processed Serving path S3 Processed -- ObjectCreated (*.parquet) --> Lambda QMJ Loader --> DynamoDB DynamoDB --> Lambda Reader --> API Gateway --> Browser Automation path EventBridge Scheduler - - -→ Glue Python Shell Daily Ingestion Data Contract Dataset Grain Output location Consumer us_prices_raw.parquet ticker + price_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/ Glue PySpark QMJ us_company_info.parquet ticker + snapshot_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/ Glue PySpark QMJ us_financials_raw.parquet ticker + report_date + period_type + snapshot_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/ Glue PySpark QMJ QMJ output Parquet One row per ticker at AS_OF_DATE processed_qmj/as_of_date=.../ Lambda QMJ Loader DynamoDB item ticker + snapshot_date Table qmj_screener Lambda Reader Architectural Principle – Event-Driven Serving. qmj_transform.py does not have PutItem or BatchWriteItem. The transform completes at S3 Processed; Lambda Loader is responsible for loading DynamoDB after detecting new Parquet files.

We will build a Lambda function that acts as the API Backend responsible for receiving the hero_id parameter sent from the browser, querying DynamoDB, and returning the JSON result.
Step Action Technical Details 1 Access AWS Console Search for the Lambda service in the search bar. 2 Initialize Function Select Functions from the left menu > Click the orange Create function button. 3 Basic Configuration Select Author from scratch. Function name: dota2-backend-api. Runtime: Select Python 3.9 (or newer). 4 Configure Permissions Expand Change default execution role > Select Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions (AWS will automatically create a secure basic Role). Click Create function. 5 Attach DynamoDB Read Permissions Go to the Configuration tab > Permissions section > Click the blue Role name link. The system will open the IAM tab. 6 Add Inline Policy Click Add permissions > Create inline policy > Select the JSON tab and paste the code below (Remember to replace YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID) > Set policy name: DynamoDB_Read_Dota2_Metrics > Click Create policy. 7 Write API Source Code Return to the Lambda Function tab > Scroll down to the Code editor, clear the default code, paste the Python Backend code below > Click the orange Deploy button. JSON Policy Code to grant read permissions to Lambda:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:GetItem" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:table/dota2_hero_metrics" } ] } Python Backend Source Code:
import json import boto3 DYNAMODB_TABLE = "dota2_hero_metrics" def lambda_handler(event, context): print("Received event:", json.dumps(event)) # 1. Extract hero_id parameter from API Gateway (Query String or Path Parameter) query_params = event.get('queryStringParameters') or {} hero_id = query_params.get('hero_id') if not hero_id: return { 'statusCode': 400, 'headers': { 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*', # Enable CORS to prevent Browser blocking errors 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, 'body': json.dumps({'error': 'The hero_id parameter is required!'}) } # 2. Query data directly from Amazon DynamoDB using Key Lookups dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='ap-southeast-1') table = dynamodb.Table(DYNAMODB_TABLE) response = table.get_item(Key={'hero_id': int(hero_id)}) item = response.get('Item') if not item: return { 'statusCode': 404, 'headers': {'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*', 'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, 'body': json.dumps({'message': f'No data found for Hero ID {hero_id}'}) } # 3. Return clean JSON response to Frontend return { 'statusCode': 200, 'headers': { 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, 'body': json.dumps(item) }

title: Pipeline Automation with Amazon EventBridge
content:
We will perform 2 main tasks: Deploy the data ingestion Python script to AWS Lambda, and set up an EventBridge Schedule to run automatically at 2:00 AM daily.
Part 1: Create Ingestion Lambda (Replacing Local Ingestion Script)
Step Action Technical Details 1 Create Lambda Function Open Lambda > Click Create function. Name: dota2-auto-ingestion. Runtime: Python 3.9. 2 Grant S3 Permissions Similar to section 5.1, go to Configuration > Permissions > Open the Role and add an Inline Policy allowing s3:PutObject on the Raw bucket. 3 Paste Source Code Paste the Python code below into the Code Editor. Replace YOUR_RAW_BUCKET with your bucket name. Click Deploy. 4 Configure Timeout Go to Configuration > General configuration > Edit. Increase Timeout from 3 seconds to 1 minute. Click Save. dota2-auto-ingestion Source Code (Using default standard library urllib instead of requests so no Lambda Layer is required):
import urllib.request import boto3 import json from datetime import datetime API_URL = "https://api.opendota.com/api/proMatches" BUCKET_NAME = "YOUR_RAW_BUCKET" PREFIX = "raw_matches" def lambda_handler(event, context): print("Starting data ingestion from OpenDota API...") req = urllib.request.Request(API_URL, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: if response.status == 200: matches = json.loads(response.read().decode()) date_str = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d") file_name = f"matches_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}.json" s3_key = f"{PREFIX}/dt={date_str}/{file_name}" s3 = boto3.client('s3') s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET_NAME, Key=s3_key, Body=json.dumps(matches), ContentType='application/json') return {"status": 200, "message": f"Successfully pushed {len(matches)} matches to S3"} else: return {"status": response.status, "message": "API invocation error"}

title: Design Step Functions Conductor
content:
To free the system from manually triggered tasks, we will use AWS Step Functions Workflow Studio to build a fully automated process in a sequential chain.
Step 1: Initialize AWS Glue Crawler to scan data Before Step Functions can orchestrate, we need an automated tool to identify new Parquet files landing on S3 to update the ledger (Data Catalog).
Step Action Technical details 1 Search service In the AWS Console search bar, type Glue and select Crawlers. 2 Create Crawler Click the Create crawler button, name it Clickstream_S3_Crawler. 3 Add data source Click Add a data source, select S3 and point the absolute path to the raw data folder: s3://your-bucket-name/data/. 4 Configure IAM permissions Select Create new IAM Role for AWS to automatically grant S3 read permissions for the Crawler. 5 Specify Database In the Output configuration section, create a new Database named clickstream_db. 6 Complete Click Create crawler to save the configuration. Step 2: Set up State Machine chain to prevent Race Condition We proceed to assemble the services into an automated chain through the intuitive drag-and-drop interface of Step Functions.
Step Action Technical details 1 Create State Machine Go to the Step Functions service -> Click Create state machine -> Select Workflow Studio (Drag and drop). 2 Drag Crawler block In the left filter, type Glue -> Drag the Glue StartCrawler block and drop it at the starting point (Start). In the right configuration column, enter the crawler name: Clickstream_S3_Crawler. 3 Insert Wait State In the left filter, type Wait -> Drag the Wait State block (clock icon) and drop it RIGHT AFTER the Crawler block. Set the time to 120 Seconds. 4 Drag Lambda block In the left filter, type Lambda -> Drag the Lambda Invoke block and drop it after the Wait block. Point the target function to the AthenaETLProcessor function (will be created in section 3.2). 5 Drag SNS block In the left filter, type SNS -> Drag the SNS Publish block and drop it at the end of the processing flow. Select the Topic ARN pointing to Pipeline_Completion_Alert prepared in Chapter 1. 6 Save and Deploy Click Save in the top right corner to save the Conductor diagram. System Error Alert (Race Condition): Adding the Wait State (120 seconds) block is a mandatory infrastructure engineering technique. AWS Glue Crawler takes an average of 1 to 2 minutes to scan the S3 hard drive and successfully update the table structure into the Data Catalog. Meanwhile, the AWS Lambda compute robot operates very quickly (takes only 3 seconds). Without the Wait State blocking block, Lambda will jump into executing the SQL query immediately while the data ledger is empty, leading to your output CSV file being completely blank.
Step 3: Schedule automatic running with Amazon EventBridge Scheduler The current AWS interface has separated the scheduling feature into a powerful dedicated tool called EventBridge Scheduler. We will use this tool to wake up the Conductor.
Step Action Technical details 1 Access Scheduler Go to the Amazon EventBridge service -> Look at the left menu, find the Scheduler section and select Schedules. 2 Create Schedule Click the Create schedule button. 3 Name it In the Schedule name box, enter the name Trigger-NewsPipeline-Hourly. 4 Configure time In the Schedule pattern section, select Recurring schedule. Continue to select Rate-based schedule, enter the number 1 and the unit as Hours (The system automatically runs once an hour). Scroll down and click Next. 5 Specify Target On the Target detail page, find and select AWS Step Functions -> Select API StartExecution. In the State machine box, point to the Conductor name you just drew in Step 2. Scroll down and click Next. 6 Permissions & Complete On the Settings page, in the Permissions section, keep the Create new role for this schedule option for AWS to automatically grant permissions. Click Create schedule.

title: Introduction
content:
Project Introduction This project builds a fully automated Serverless system that:
Automatically collects YouTube comments daily via the YouTube Data API v3. Analyzes sentiment using Generative AI (Amazon Bedrock - Claude 3) with context and sarcasm understanding. Stores results in Amazon S3 (Data Lake) and Amazon DynamoDB. Visualizes insights through interactive dashboards on Amazon QuickSight. Core Architecture The system follows a Decoupled Event-Driven architecture:
Component Service Role Data Collection AWS Lambda (Producer) Fetches YouTube video list by keyword Message Queue Amazon SQS Buffers video IDs, preventing API overload AI Processing AWS Lambda (Consumer + Transformer) Fetches comments and calls Bedrock for analysis Data Storage Amazon S3 + DynamoDB Data Lake and deduplication tracking Analytics Amazon Athena + QuickSight SQL queries and dashboard visualization Automation Amazon EventBridge Triggers pipeline daily at 8:00 AM Why This Architecture? Problem: YouTube Data API v3 has a strict daily quota. Calling it in a single synchronous function risks timeouts and quota exhaustion.
Solution: Separate the workload into 3 Lambda functions connected via SQS queues:
Producer_Lambda → fetches video list, pushes IDs to SQS Consumer_Lambda → reads from SQS, fetches comments, calls Bedrock Transformer_Lambda → reads raw S3 output, transforms into Athena-queryable Parquet

title: Create Lambda QMJ Loader with S3 Trigger
content:
qmj_transform.py outputs Parquet files to processed_qmj/as_of_date=YYYY-MM-DD/. This section configures Lambda QMJ Loader to ingest newly processed files.
This Lambda function operates in two modes:
Mode Invocation Method Purpose s3_trigger S3 automatically sends event notifications when new .parquet files arrive Ingests new incremental output from Glue PySpark backfill Lambda Test Event or Invoke API Scans the entire processed_qmj/ directory and loads historical QMJ scores Architectural Principle – Source Boundary. This is not a Glue Publisher Job. S3 is the event source, Lambda is the compute layer that loads the Serving Store, and DynamoDB is the read-optimized projection for the website.
Prepare Deployment Package The source imports awswrangler, pandas, and pyarrow as dependencies. The default Lambda runtime does not include these packages, so you need to attach a Lambda Layer or upload a deployment package compatible with the Python runtime and architecture you are using.
Step Action Technical Details 1 Open AWS CloudShell or a Lambda-compatible build environment Used to create a Linux-compatible package 2 Create a package directory Package must contain lambda_function.py and dependencies 3 Install dependencies Install awswrangler, pandas, pyarrow into the package or a Layer 4 Copy Lambda source Save the source below as lambda_function.py 5 Zip the package Upload the zip to Lambda in the next step # Run in a Lambda-compatible build environment. mkdir qmj-loader-package cd qmj-loader-package # Install Lambda source dependencies into the package. python -m pip install --target . awswrangler pandas pyarrow cp ../lambda_qmj_loader.py lambda_function.py # Create the upload file for Lambda. zip -r ../qmj-loader.zip . Create Lambda Function Step Action Technical Details 1 AWS Lambda → Functions → Create function Select Author from scratch 2 Function name Enter qmj-s3-to-dynamodb-loader 3 Runtime Select the Python runtime that matches your deployment package/Lambda Layer 4 Architecture Keep consistent with the package or Layer you built 5 Execution role Select Use an existing role → LambdaQMJLoaderRole 6 Select Create function Open the new function 7 Code → Upload from → .zip file Upload qmj-loader.zip 8 Runtime settings → Edit Handler is lambda_function.lambda_handler 9 Configuration → General configuration Increase the timeout to allow enough time to read Parquet and write all tickers 10 Select Deploy Save the function and package Add Environment Variables Step Action Technical Details 1 Lambda → Configuration → Environment variables Select Edit 2 Add TABLE_NAME Value: qmj_screener 3 Add PROCESSED_BUCKET Value: stock-screener-processed-your-name 4 Add PROCESSED_PREFIX Value: processed_qmj/ 5 Select Save Do not save access keys here Create S3 Trigger Step Action Technical Details 1 Lambda → Function overview → Add trigger Select trigger source S3 2 Bucket Select stock-screener-processed-your-name 3 Event type Select All object create events 4 Prefix Enter processed_qmj/ 5 Suffix Enter .parquet 6 Recursive invocation Enable the acknowledgement if the Console shows it — Lambda does not write objects back to S3 so no loop is created 7 Select Add S3 event notification will invoke Lambda When Glue PySpark writes output as shown below, the S3 trigger only forwards the part-...parquet file; the _SUCCESS file is ignored by the suffix filter and Lambda code.
processed_qmj/ └── as_of_date=2026-07-06/ ├── part-00000-....snappy.parquet ← Lambda trigger └── _SUCCESS ← ignored Lambda Loader Source Code The import json line is included because the source needs json.dumps(response) when failed_files are present.
import json import os import re import math import boto3 import urllib.parse import awswrangler as wr import pandas as pd from datetime import date, datetime from decimal import Decimal from numbers import Integral, Real TABLE_NAME = os.environ.get("TABLE_NAME", "qmj_screener") PROCESSED_BUCKET = os.environ.get( "PROCESSED_BUCKET", "stock-screener-processed-your-name" ) PROCESSED_PREFIX = os.environ.get( "PROCESSED_PREFIX", "processed_qmj/" ) dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb") s3 = boto3.client("s3") table = dynamodb.Table(TABLE_NAME) def to_dynamodb_value(value): # Normalize Pandas/NumPy values to types accepted by DynamoDB. if value is None: return None try: if bool(pd.isna(value)): return None except Exception: pass if isinstance(value, (datetime, date)): return value.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") if isinstance(value, bool): return value if isinstance(value, Decimal): return value if isinstance(value, Integral): return Decimal(str(int(value))) if isinstance(value, Real): number = float(value) if not math.isfinite(number): return None return Decimal(str(number)) if isinstance(value, str): return value return str(value) def extract_as_of_date(s3_key): # Extract partition date from processed_qmj/as_of_date=YYYY-MM-DD/. match = re.search( r"(?:^|/)as_of_date=(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})(?:/|$)", s3_key ) if not match: raise ValueError(f"as_of_date not found in key: {s3_key}") as_of_date = match.group(1) datetime.strptime(as_of_date, "%Y-%m-%d") return as_of_date def load_parquet_to_dynamodb(bucket, key): as_of_date = extract_as_of_date(key) s3_path = f"s3://{bucket}/{key}" df = wr.s3.read_parquet(path=s3_path) if df.empty: return 0, 0 if "ticker" not in df.columns: raise ValueError(f"File does not have ticker column: {s3_path}") loaded_rows = 0 skipped_rows = 0 columns = list(df.columns) # Overwrite by ticker + snapshot_date so retried events do not create duplicate logical items. with table.batch_writer( overwrite_by_pkeys=["ticker", "snapshot_date"] ) as batch: for values in df.itertuples(index=False, name=None): item = {} for column, value in zip(columns, values): clean_value = to_dynamodb_value(value) if clean_value is not None: item[column] = clean_value ticker = str(item.get("ticker", "")).strip().upper() if not ticker: skipped_rows += 1 continue item["ticker"] = ticker item["snapshot_date"] = as_of_date item["as_of_date"] = as_of_date item["source_s3_key"] = key batch.put_item(Item=item) loaded_rows += 1 return loaded_rows, skipped_rows def get_existing_parquet_files(bucket, prefix): keys = [] paginator = s3.get_paginator("list_objects_v2") for page in paginator.paginate(Bucket=bucket, Prefix=prefix): for obj in page.get("Contents", []): key = obj["Key"] if key.endswith(".parquet"): keys.append(key) return sorted(keys) def process_files(bucket, keys): processed_files = 0 loaded_rows = 0 skipped_rows = 0 failed_files = [] for key in keys: try: loaded, skipped = load_parquet_to_dynamodb(bucket, key) processed_files += 1 loaded_rows += loaded skipped_rows += skipped except Exception as error: failed_files.append({"key": key, "error": str(error)}) return { "processed_files": processed_files, "loaded_rows": loaded_rows, "skipped_rows": skipped_rows, "failed_files": failed_files } def lambda_handler(event, context): event = event or {} # Manual backfill mode: scan all QMJ Parquet files in Processed Zone. if event.get("mode") == "backfill": bucket = event.get("bucket", PROCESSED_BUCKET) prefix = event.get("prefix", PROCESSED_PREFIX) keys = get_existing_parquet_files(bucket, prefix) if not keys: return { "mode": "backfill", "processed_files": 0, "loaded_rows": 0, "skipped_rows": 0, "failed_files": [] } result = process_files(bucket, keys) result["mode"] = "backfill" result["total_parquet_files_found"] = len(keys) return result # S3 trigger mode: filter ObjectCreated events in the Processed QMJ prefix. keys_by_bucket = {} for record in event.get("Records", []): if record.get("eventSource") != "aws:s3": continue if not record.get("eventName", "").startswith("ObjectCreated:"): continue bucket = record["s3"]["bucket"]["name"] key = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(record["s3"]["object"]["key"]) if not key.startswith(PROCESSED_PREFIX) or not key.endswith(".parquet"): continue keys_by_bucket.setdefault(bucket, []).append(key) total_processed_files = 0 total_loaded_rows = 0 total_skipped_rows = 0 failed_files = [] for bucket, keys in keys_by_bucket.items(): result = process_files(bucket, keys) total_processed_files += result["processed_files"] total_loaded_rows += result["loaded_rows"] total_skipped_rows += result["skipped_rows"] failed_files.extend(result["failed_files"]) response = { "mode": "s3_trigger", "processed_files": total_processed_files, "loaded_rows": total_loaded_rows, "skipped_rows": total_skipped_rows, "failed_files": failed_files } if failed_files: raise Exception(json.dumps(response)) return response Test Lambda Loader Step Action Technical Details 1 Lambda → Test → Create new event Use this test for historical QMJ data already on S3 2 Event name Enter backfill-processed-qmj 3 Paste event JSON below No need to mock an S3 event 4 Select Test Lambda lists all Parquet files under the prefix 5 Open Monitor tab → View CloudWatch logs Verify processed_files, loaded_rows, failed_files 6 DynamoDB → Explore table items Verify ticker and snapshot_date { "mode": "backfill" }

title: Deploy Daily Ingestion via Glue Python Shell
content:
Daily Ingestion fetches the S&P 500 ticker list from Wikipedia, pulls market data from Yahoo Finance via yfinance, and writes three Raw datasets.
us_prices_raw.parquet us_company_info.parquet us_financials_raw.parquet Unlike local backfill execution, this step creates an AWS Glue Python Shell Job and pastes source code directly into the Glue Script editor.
Prerequisites Before Job Creation Step Action Technical Details 1 Verify Raw Bucket The active S3 bucket is stock-screener-raw-khanh 2 Verify IAM Role Role AWSGlueServiceRole-StockScreener must have write permissions to raw_us_market/* 3 Verify Internet access The Job must be able to call Wikipedia, Yahoo Finance, and PyPI to install additional packages 4 Prepare source code Copy the complete daily_ingestion.py code at the bottom of this page 5 Do not hardcode credentials boto3.client("s3") automatically uses temporary credentials supplied by the Glue Role Architectural Principle – Direct Editor. Glue Studio allows creating a new Python Shell script and writing code directly in the Script editor. You do not need to manually upload the script file to S3. AWS Glue still manages the Script Location for the Job at the service layer, but no manual operations with a glue-scripts/ directory are required.
Create Glue Python Shell Job and Paste Code Directly Step Action Technical Details 1 Open AWS Console → AWS Glue Enter the AWS Glue management page 2 Select ETL jobs or Jobs Open the Glue Job list 3 In the job creation section, select Script editor Do not select Visual ETL or Notebook 4 Select Engine Python shell and Start fresh Do not select Upload and edit an existing script 5 Select Create Script Glue Studio opens the Script editor with boilerplate code 6 In the Script tab Delete all boilerplate code 7 Paste source daily_ingestion.py Paste the entire file from the end of this section 8 Open tab Job details Configure runtime, Role and package dependencies 9 Set Job name Use us-stock-daily-ingestion 10 Select IAM Role Select AWSGlueServiceRole-StockScreener 11 Verify Job type Must be Python shell 12 Select Python Shell runtime Select the runtime you have tested for compatibility with your dependencies Add Python Package Dependencies The code uses yfinance, pandas, requests, pyarrow, and lxml. Add these packages using Job parameters.
Step Action Technical Details 1 Open Glue Job us-stock-daily-ingestion Go to the Job details tab 2 Find Job parameters section May be located under Advanced properties depending on the Console interface 3 Select Add new parameter Create a new parameter 4 Enter Key --additional-python-modules 5 Enter Value yfinance,pandas,requests,pyarrow,lxml 6 Select Save Glue uses pip to install packages at Job startup 7 Select Run Check CloudWatch Logs to confirm packages installed successfully Key: --additional-python-modules Value: yfinance,pandas,requests,pyarrow,lxml Verify Job Configuration Before Running Attribute Value to verify Job name us-stock-daily-ingestion Job type Python shell IAM Role AWSGlueServiceRole-StockScreener Raw Bucket stock-screener-raw-khanh Raw Prefix raw_us_market Python modules yfinance,pandas,requests,pyarrow,lxml Test limit LIMIT_TICKERS_FOR_TEST = None to run the full S&P 500 AWS credentials No Access Key or Secret Key in code Partition and Dedupe Rules in Source Code Dataset Dedupe key Partition path Purpose Prices ticker + price_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/us_prices_raw.parquet Save by most recent trading date Company Info ticker + snapshot_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/us_company_info.parquet Save by Glue Job run date Financials ticker+report_date+period_type+snapshot_date raw_us_market/YYYY/MM/DD/us_financials_raw.parquet Save by Glue Job run date # Example: Job runs on Sunday 2026-07-06. # The most recent trading session returned by yfinance is Friday 2026-07-03. raw_us_market/2026/07/03/us_prices_raw.parquet raw_us_market/2026/07/06/us_company_info.parquet raw_us_market/2026/07/06/us_financials_raw.parquet Verify Result on Amazon S3 Step Action Technical Details 1 Amazon S3 → stock-screener-raw-khanh Open Raw Bucket 2 Open raw_us_market/ View partitions by year/month/date 3 Find us_prices_raw.parquet Partition uses the most recent trading date 4 Find us_company_info.parquet Partition uses the Job run date 5 Find us_financials_raw.parquet Partition uses the Job run date 6 Open CloudWatch Logs for the Job Cross-reference the Saved to S3 log with the actual objects Architectural Principle – Schema parity. Daily Ingestion casts all metrics to float64 and all date fields to string before writing Parquet. Backfill applies the same rules. This is the primary defense layer against schema drift, especially when yfinance changes column types or omits Adj Close, Dividends, or Stock Splits.
Full source: daily_ingestion.py import io import time import traceback from datetime import datetime import boto3 import pandas as pd import requests import yfinance as yf # ========================================== # BASE CONFIGURATION # ========================================== BUCKET_NAME = "stock-screener-raw-khanh" RAW_PREFIX = "raw_us_market" # Set to None to run the full S&P 500 LIMIT_TICKERS_FOR_TEST = None s3 = boto3.client("s3") # ========================================== # FETCH TICKERS (SAME AS BACKFILL) # ========================================== def get_sp500_tickers(): url = "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_S%26P_500_companies" headers = { "User-Agent": ( "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) " "AppleWebKit/537.36 Chrome/120.0 Safari/537.36" ) } response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30) response.raise_for_status() df_sp500 = pd.read_html(response.text)[0] return [ticker.replace(".", "-") for ticker in df_sp500["Symbol"].tolist()] # ========================================== # PARQUET HANDLER (IDENTICAL TO BACKFILL) # ========================================== def to_parquet_bytes(df: pd.DataFrame) -> bytes: """ Convert a DataFrame to Parquet compatible with AWS Glue. """ output_df = df.copy() for column_name in output_df.columns: if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(output_df[column_name]): date_series = output_df[column_name] if isinstance(date_series.dtype, pd.DatetimeTZDtype): date_series = date_series.dt.tz_localize(None) # Format by column name, same as backfill if column_name in ["price_date", "report_date", "snapshot_date"]: output_df[column_name] = date_series.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") else: output_df[column_name] = date_series.dt.strftime( "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" ) buf = io.BytesIO() output_df.to_parquet( buf, index=False, compression="snappy", engine="pyarrow", version="1.0" ) return buf.getvalue() def put_df(df: pd.DataFrame, key: str) -> tuple: """Normalize data types then push Parquet to S3.""" if df.empty: print(f"⚠️ Skipping empty file: {key}") return 0, 0 output_df = df.copy() # Cast metrics to Float64 to avoid Integer vs Double errors in Spark. numeric_columns = [] if "us_prices_raw" in key: numeric_columns = [ "open", "high", "low", "close", "adj_close", "volume", "dividends", "stock_splits" ] elif "us_company_info" in key: numeric_columns = [ "current_market_cap", "shares_outstanding", "enterprise_value", "float_shares", "beta", "trailing_pe", "return_on_equity", "debt_to_equity", "earnings_growth", "revenue_growth" ] elif "us_financials_raw" in key: numeric_columns = [ "revenue", "net_income", "shareholders_equity", "total_assets", "total_debt", "operating_cash_flow", "capital_expenditure", "free_cash_flow", "stock_repurchased", "stock_issued" ] for col in numeric_columns: if col in output_df.columns: output_df[col] = ( pd.to_numeric(output_df[col], errors="coerce") .astype("float64") ) # Cast date fields to string for stable Spark/Glue schema reading. for date_col in [ "price_date", "report_date", "snapshot_date", "ingested_at" ]: if date_col in output_df.columns: output_df[date_col] = output_df[date_col].astype("string") s3.put_object( Bucket=BUCKET_NAME, Key=key, Body=to_parquet_bytes(output_df), ContentType="application/octet-stream" ) print(f"✅ Saved to S3: {key} | Rows: {len(output_df)}") return len(output_df), len(output_df.columns) # ========================================== # DAILY CRAWL FUNCTION # ========================================== def run_yfinance_full_ingestion(): now = datetime.now() # Company Info and Financials are partitioned by pipeline run date. yyyy = now.strftime("%Y") mm = now.strftime("%m") dd = now.strftime("%d") current_snapshot_date = now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") ingested_at = now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") raw_prefix_today = f"{RAW_PREFIX}/{yyyy}/{mm}/{dd}" print("=== START DAILY STOCK INGESTION ===") print(f"Snapshot date: {current_snapshot_date}") all_tickers = get_sp500_tickers() if LIMIT_TICKERS_FOR_TEST is not None: all_tickers = all_tickers[:LIMIT_TICKERS_FOR_TEST] all_prices, all_financials, all_info = [], [], [] def get_val(df, possible_rows, report_date): if df is None or df.empty: return None for row_name in possible_rows: if row_name in df.index: try: return df.loc[row_name, report_date] except Exception: return None return None for i, t in enumerate(all_tickers, 1): print(f"\n🔄 Processing ticker: {t} ({i}/{len(all_tickers)})") try: stock = yf.Ticker(t) # --------------------------------------------------------- # 1. FETCH MOST RECENT TRADING SESSION PRICE # --------------------------------------------------------- try: # Fetch 5 days to capture the most recent session even on weekends. df_price = stock.history(period="5d", auto_adjust=False) if not df_price.empty: df_price = df_price.reset_index() if "Date" in df_price.columns: df_price = df_price.rename( columns={"Date": "price_date"} ) if "Datetime" in df_price.columns: df_price = df_price.rename( columns={"Datetime": "price_date"} ) df_price["price_date"] = ( pd.to_datetime(df_price["price_date"]) .dt.tz_localize(None) ) rename_map = { "Open": "open", "High": "high", "Low": "low", "Close": "close", "Adj Close": "adj_close", "Volume": "volume", "Dividends": "dividends", "Stock Splits": "stock_splits" } df_price = df_price.rename(columns=rename_map) # When yfinance does not return Adj Close, use Close as fallback. if ( "adj_close" not in df_price.columns and "close" in df_price.columns ): df_price["adj_close"] = df_price["close"] df_price["ticker"] = t df_price["snapshot_date"] = current_snapshot_date df_price["ingested_at"] = ingested_at # Save only the most recent trading session for this ticker. latest_date = df_price["price_date"].max() df_price_latest = df_price[ df_price["price_date"] == latest_date ].copy() expected_cols = [ "price_date", "ticker", "open", "high", "low", "close", "adj_close", "volume", "dividends", "stock_splits", "snapshot_date", "ingested_at" ] final_cols = [ c for c in expected_cols if c in df_price_latest.columns ] df_price_latest = df_price_latest[final_cols] if not df_price_latest.empty: all_prices.append(df_price_latest) print( " ✅ Most recent session: " f"{latest_date.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}" ) else: print(" ⚠️ Price data is empty.") except Exception as e: print(f" ⚠️ Error fetching Prices: {e}") # --------------------------------------------------------- # 2. FETCH COMPANY INFO # --------------------------------------------------------- try: info = stock.info or {} except Exception: info = {} try: fast_info = stock.fast_info or {} market_cap = ( fast_info.get("marketCap") or info.get("marketCap", 0) ) except Exception: fast_info = {} market_cap = info.get("marketCap", 0) if market_cap: try: info_dict = { "ticker": t, "snapshot_date": current_snapshot_date, "company_name": ( info.get("shortName") or info.get("longName") or t ), "exchange": info.get("exchange"), "sector": info.get("sector"), "industry": info.get("industry"), "country": info.get("country"), "currency": info.get("currency"), "website": info.get("website"), "current_market_cap": market_cap, "shares_outstanding": info.get("sharesOutstanding"), "enterprise_value": info.get("enterpriseValue"), "float_shares": info.get("floatShares"), "beta": info.get("beta"), "trailing_pe": info.get("trailingPE"), "return_on_equity": info.get("returnOnEquity"), "debt_to_equity": info.get("debtToEquity"), "earnings_growth": info.get("earningsGrowth"), "revenue_growth": info.get("revenueGrowth"), "ingested_at": ingested_at } all_info.append(info_dict) print(" ✅ Company info") except Exception as e: print(f" ⚠️ Error fetching Company Info: {e}") # --------------------------------------------------------- # 3. FETCH FINANCIALS # --------------------------------------------------------- try: income = stock.quarterly_income_stmt balance = stock.quarterly_balance_sheet cashflow = stock.quarterly_cashflow period_type = "quarterly" # Fall back to annual if quarterly data is unavailable. if income.empty and balance.empty and cashflow.empty: income = stock.income_stmt balance = stock.balance_sheet cashflow = stock.cashflow period_type = "annual" report_dates = set() for statement in [income, balance, cashflow]: if statement is not None and not statement.empty: report_dates.update(statement.columns.tolist()) for report_date in report_dates: report_date_str = pd.Timestamp( report_date ).strftime("%Y-%m-%d") financial_dict = { "ticker": t, "report_date": report_date_str, "snapshot_date": current_snapshot_date, "period_type": period_type, "revenue": get_val( income, ["Total Revenue", "Operating Revenue"], report_date ), "net_income": get_val( income, [ "Net Income", "Net Income Common Stockholders" ], report_date ), "shareholders_equity": get_val( balance, [ "Stockholders Equity", "Stockholders' Equity", "Common Stock Equity" ], report_date ), "total_assets": get_val( balance, ["Total Assets"], report_date ), "total_debt": get_val( balance, [ "Total Debt", "Total Debt And Capital Lease Obligation" ], report_date ), "operating_cash_flow": get_val( cashflow, ["Operating Cash Flow"], report_date ), "capital_expenditure": get_val( cashflow, ["Capital Expenditure", "Purchase Of PPE"], report_date ), "free_cash_flow": get_val( cashflow, ["Free Cash Flow"], report_date ), "stock_repurchased": get_val( cashflow, [ "Repurchase Of Capital Stock", "Repurchase Of Stock" ], report_date ), "stock_issued": get_val( cashflow, [ "Issuance Of Capital Stock", "Issuance Of Stock" ], report_date ), "ingested_at": ingested_at } all_financials.append(financial_dict) if report_dates: print( " ✅ Financials: " f"{len(report_dates)} reporting periods" ) except Exception as e: print(f" ⚠️ Error fetching Financials: {e}") except Exception as e: print(f"⚠️ Critical error processing ticker {t}: {e}") time.sleep(0.5) print("\n=== MERGING DATA AND UPLOADING TO S3 ===") # 1. PRICES: Partition by actual trading date. if all_prices: df_prices = pd.concat(all_prices, ignore_index=True) df_prices["price_date_dt"] = pd.to_datetime( df_prices["price_date"], errors="coerce" ) df_prices = df_prices.dropna(subset=["price_date_dt"]) df_prices = df_prices.drop_duplicates( subset=["ticker", "price_date"], keep="last" ) for trade_date, df_one_day in df_prices.groupby( df_prices["price_date_dt"].dt.normalize() ): p_yyyy = trade_date.strftime("%Y") p_mm = trade_date.strftime("%m") p_dd = trade_date.strftime("%d") price_prefix = f"{RAW_PREFIX}/{p_yyyy}/{p_mm}/{p_dd}" df_save = df_one_day.drop(columns=["price_date_dt"]) put_df( df_save, f"{price_prefix}/us_prices_raw.parquet" ) # 2. COMPANY INFO: Partition by Glue Job run date. if all_info: df_info = pd.DataFrame(all_info) df_info = df_info.drop_duplicates( subset=["ticker", "snapshot_date"], keep="last" ) put_df( df_info, f"{raw_prefix_today}/us_company_info.parquet" ) # 3. FINANCIALS: Partition by Glue Job run date. if all_financials: df_financials = pd.DataFrame(all_financials) df_financials = df_financials.drop_duplicates( subset=[ "ticker", "report_date", "period_type", "snapshot_date" ], keep="last" ) put_df( df_financials, f"{raw_prefix_today}/us_financials_raw.parquet" ) print("\n🎉 Daily data Ingestion complete!") if __name__ == "__main__": try: run_yfinance_full_ingestion() except Exception as e: print("[CRITICAL ERROR]", str(e)) print(traceback.format_exc()) raise

content:
To provide the system with input data for AI training, I have built a Clickstream data simulator using Python. This simulator models the behavior of 3 user groups (Personas) with different weights, creating a dataset with realistic patterns.
Step 0: Create dedicated User and Get security key (Best Practice) To ensure absolute safety for the system (Principle of Least Privilege), we will NOT use the Admin account. Instead, I will create a dedicated anonymous IAM User that only has permission to push data to Kinesis Firehose.
Step Action Technical details 1 Access IAM In the AWS Console, type to search IAM -> Select Users -> Click Create user. 2 Identify User Name the User Clickstream-Data-Pusher and click Next. 3 Authorize (Least Privilege) Select Attach policies directly. Find and check the AmazonKinesisFirehoseFullAccess policy. Click Next -> Create user. 4 Open security tab Click on the newly created user name Clickstream-Data-Pusher, switch to the Security credentials tab. 5 Create new key Scroll down to the Access keys section, click the Create access key button. Select Local code, confirm and click Next. 6 Store key The screen displays Access key and Secret access key. Please copy these two strings to paste into the Python code below. title: ETL Processing with Lambda and Athena
content:
This article guides you to configure the core data processing block (Core ETL Compute Layer). We will write a Python script executing on AWS Lambda to control the Amazon Athena service to run Serverless SQL queries, cast Parquet data types, and extract timestamps to native integers for AI.
AWS Lambda compute function configuration guide Step Action Technical details 1 Initialize function Go to the AWS Lambda service -> Click Create function -> Select Author from scratch. 2 Basic setup Name the function AthenaETLProcessor. Select the language Runtime as Python 3.12. 3 Configure time Switch to the Configuration tab -> General configuration section -> Click Edit, increase the Timeout parameter to a minimum of 2 minutes (to avoid the function being interrupted while waiting for Athena to export the file). 4 Grant system permissions In the Permissions section, click on the Execution Role link to open the IAM interface. Proceed to attach 2 standard permission policies: AmazonAthenaFullAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess. ETL Processing Source Code (Python & Serverless SQL) Please return to the Code tab of the Lambda function, clear the default code, paste the entire Enterprise standard source code block below and click the orange Deploy button:
import boto3 import time def lambda_handler(event, context): athena_client = boto3.client('athena') # Define database configuration and destination folder DATABASE = 'clickstream_db' # ⚠️ Note: Accurately replace your S3 Bucket Data Lake name in the line below OUTPUT_LOCATION = 's3://your-clickstream-datalake-bucket-name/personalize_data/' # SQL query to extract Parquet, capitalize column headers and convert time format to UNIX Epoch Time query = """ SELECT user_id AS USER_ID, page_url AS ITEM_ID, CAST(to_unixtime(CAST(event_timestamp AS timestamp)) AS bigint) AS "TIMESTAMP", event_type AS EVENT_TYPE, device_os AS DEVICE_OS FROM "clickstream_db"."crawled_data" WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL; """ print("🚀 Waking up Amazon Athena to execute Serverless SQL ETL query...") response = athena_client.start_query_execution( QueryString=query, QueryExecutionContext={'Database': DATABASE}, ResultConfiguration={'OutputLocation': OUTPUT_LOCATION} ) query_execution_id = response['QueryExecutionId'] # Polling Loop technique to check Athena's asynchronous status state = 'RUNNING' while state in ['RUNNING', 'QUEUED']: check_status = athena_client.get_query_execution(QueryExecutionId=query_execution_id) state = check_status['QueryExecution']['Status']['State'] if state in ['RUNNING', 'QUEUED']: time.sleep(2) if state == 'SUCCEEDED': print(f"✅ Excellent! The standardized CSV data for AI has safely landed at: {OUTPUT_LOCATION}") return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': 'ETL Data Transformation Successful!'} else: raise Exception(f"❌ Athena ETL pipeline collapsed at error state: {state}")

title: Cloud Infrastructure Deployment
content:
Deploy the System on AWS In this chapter, we will start configuring the Serverless services on the AWS Management Console. Our deployment strategy follows a bottom-up approach, working from the end of the data flow back to the beginning:
Storage & Alerting (DynamoDB, SNS): Prepare the journey data “storage” and set up the “loudspeaker” to send email notifications when incidents occur. Processing & Buffering (Lambda, SQS): Create a queue to buffer high-speed data, while writing a function to handle temperature checking logic. Ingestion (IoT Core): Create a virtual device (Thing), provision security certificates, and configure a Rule to route the data stream into the queue. Deploying in this order allows services to easily identify and grant permissions to each other without encountering “resource not found” errors.
Contents Initialize DynamoDB & SNS Configure SQS & Lambda Set Up IoT Core

title: Create Amazon SQS & Write AWS Lambda
content:
1. Create Amazon SQS Queue Amazon SQS acts as the “shock absorber” for the system. When thousands of trucks send data simultaneously, SQS will buffer all of it and hold the messages in the queue for Lambda to process gradually, preventing overload.
Search for and open the Simple Queue Service (SQS) service. Click Create queue. Configure the queue: Type: Select Standard. Name: IoT_Fleet_Queue. Keep the default settings and click Create queue. Important: After creation, copy the queue URL (in the format https://sqs...) for use in the IoT Rule configuration step later. 2. Write the AWS Lambda Processing Function This Lambda function is the “brain” of the system. It will automatically trigger when data is in SQS, analyze the temperature, and decide whether to send an alert.
Step A: Create the Lambda Function
Open the Lambda service > Click Create function. Select Author from scratch: Function name: IoT_Process_Data. Runtime: Select Python 3.9 or newer. Click Create function. Step B: Grant Permissions For Lambda to read from SQS, write to DynamoDB, and send messages via SNS, you need to grant it permissions:
Go to the Configuration tab > Permissions > Click the Role name to open the IAM interface. Click Add permissions > Attach policies. Find and add the permissions: AmazonSQSFullAccess, AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess, AmazonSNSFullAccess. Step C: Write the Processing Code Return to the Code tab of Lambda and paste the following code (replace YOUR_SNS_TOPIC_ARN with the ARN you copied in lesson 2.1):
import json import boto3 from decimal import Decimal dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') sns = boto3.client('sns') table = dynamodb.Table('IoT_Fleet_Data') SNS_TOPIC_ARN = 'YOUR_SNS_TOPIC_ARN' # Replace with your SNS Topic ARN def lambda_handler(event, context): for record in event['Records']: # 1. Read data from SQS body = json.loads(record['body'], parse_float=Decimal) truck_id = body['truck_id'] temp = body['temperature'] # 2. Check temperature condition (> 8 degrees C) if temp > Decimal('8.0'): message = f"ALERT: Truck {truck_id} has abnormal temperature: {temp}°C!" sns.publish(TopicArn=SNS_TOPIC_ARN, Message=message, Subject="Vaccine Temperature Alert") # 3. Save to DynamoDB table.put_item(Item=body) return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': 'Processing successful'} Step D: Add Trigger
Click Add trigger > Select SQS. Select the IoT_Fleet_Queue queue just created. Click Add.

title: IoT Fleet Monitoring System
content:
The Problem In the medical transport (vaccines) or frozen food industry, maintaining a stable temperature is a matter of survival. Manual monitoring is impossible with thousands of moving trucks, and just one cooling system failure can cause massive losses.
Serverless Architecture (Event-Driven) The system is designed following the Event-Driven Architecture model with 3 main layers:
Ingestion Layer: Collects real-time GPS and temperature data from IoT devices on the trucks. Processing & Buffering Layer: Buffers the massive data stream and automatically processes logic to detect anomalies. Storage & Alerting Layer: Stores time-series data and triggers emergency alerts. Technology Highlights AWS IoT Core: A secure gateway that receives MQTT data from thousands of devices. Amazon SQS: A “Shock absorber” (Buffer) that aggregates data, preventing system overload. AWS Lambda: Runs serverless Python code to process logic without managing servers. Amazon DynamoDB: A NoSQL Database that stores journey data at super high speed. Amazon SNS: Pushes emergency alerts via Email when the temperature exceeds the threshold.

title: Verify Data Flow & Alerts
content:

Return to the AWS Console and open DynamoDB. Select Explore items from the left menu. Select your IoT_Fleet_Data table. Click the Run (or Scan) button. You will see a stream of records (Items) appear with complete information: truck_id, temperature, latitude, longitude, and timestamp_ms. Data is updated continuously in real-time!
2. Check Emergency Alert Email In the simulator source code, the temperature is set to fluctuate randomly. If any truck has a temperature exceeding 8.0°C, the Lambda function will immediately trigger SNS.
Open your personal Email inbox (the Email registered in Lesson 2.1). You will see alert emails arriving with the subject: Vaccine Temperature Alert. The email content will specifically identify which truck is experiencing an issue and what the current temperature is.

title: Write IoT Simulator Source Code
content:
Create the simulator source code file We will create a Python file that acts as a smart sensor on the truck. [cite_start]This file is responsible for simulating the journey data of 10 trucks and sending it to the AWS Cloud via the MQTT protocol. [cite: 1]
Open the VS Code editor. Create a new file named truck_simulator.py. Copy and paste the code below into the file: import time import json import random from AWSIoTPythonSDK.MQTTLib import AWSIoTMQTTClient # ========================================== # 🔴 PARAMETER CONFIGURATION (WILL BE UPDATED IN CHAPTER 2) # ========================================== # This Endpoint will be obtained from AWS IoT Core Settings IOT_ENDPOINT = "YOUR_AWS_IOT_ENDPOINT" # Path to security certificates PATH_TO_ROOT_CA = "certs/AmazonRootCA1.pem" PATH_TO_CERT = "certs/your-certificate.pem.crt" PATH_TO_PRIVATE_KEY = "certs/your-private.pem.key" CLIENT_ID = "Vaccine_Fleet_Simulator" TOPIC = "telemetry/trucks" # Create a simulated list of 10 trucks with origin coordinates TRUCKS = [{"id": f"T-{100+i}", "lat": 10.7626 + (i * 0.01), "lon": 106.6602 - (i * 0.01)} for i in range(10)] # ========================================== # INITIALIZE SECURE MQTT CONNECTION # ========================================== myMQTTClient = AWSIoTMQTTClient(CLIENT_ID) myMQTTClient.configureEndpoint(IOT_ENDPOINT, 8883) myMQTTClient.configureCredentials(PATH_TO_ROOT_CA, PATH_TO_PRIVATE_KEY, PATH_TO_CERT) print(f"Connecting to AWS IoT Core...") # ========================================== # DATA SENDING LOOP (1 SECOND/TIME) # ========================================== try: myMQTTClient.connect() print("✅ Connection successful!\n") while True: for truck in TRUCKS: # Generate random data for temperature and position data = { "truck_id": truck["id"], "temperature": round(random.uniform(2.0, 8.0), 2), "latitude": round(truck["lat"] + random.uniform(-0.001, 0.001), 6), "longitude": round(truck["lon"] + random.uniform(-0.001, 0.001), 6), "timestamp_ms": int(time.time() * 1000) } payload = json.dumps(data) myMQTTClient.publish(TOPIC, payload, 1) print(f"[{truck['id']}] Sent: {payload}") time.sleep(1) except KeyboardInterrupt: print("\n🛑 Stopped sending data.") myMQTTClient.disconnect() Save the file to your project directory. title: Create IAM Role & Enable AI
content:
In AWS, services are isolated by default and are not permitted to communicate with each other. To allow Lambda to call AI Bedrock, read/write files on S3, and run Athena queries, we must grant it an identity card called an IAM Role.
Additionally, we need to “wake up” the Claude 3 model on Amazon Bedrock before using it in code.
1. Enable Amazon Bedrock (Claude 3 Haiku) Good news: Since 2026, AWS has simplified model permission granting to the maximum extent possible through the Auto-enablement mechanism at the account level!
Log in to the AWS Console and ensure you are in the N. Virginia (us-east-1) or Oregon (us-west-2) Region. Access the Amazon Bedrock service. In the left menu, find Playgrounds and select Chat (or Text). Click the Select model button -> Select provider Anthropic -> Select Claude 3 Haiku. Type a test greeting (e.g., “Hello Claude”) and click Send. AWS will automatically approve and activate the model for you instantly! (Note: If your account is brand new and AWS displays a form requesting Submit use case details, simply fill in: Project name, Website (can be a Github link), and Description as “Social media data analysis for educational purposes” then click Submit.)
2. Create IAM Role for Ingestor Lambda The Ingestor function is responsible for scraping raw data and writing to the Data Lake (S3), while also marking records in DynamoDB.
Access AWS IAM -> Select Roles in the left menu -> Click Create role. Trusted entity type: Select AWS service. Use case: Select Lambda -> Click Next. In the search box (Permissions policies), find and check 4 permissions: AmazonS3FullAccess AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (Required permission to write activity logs) AmazonSQSFullAccess Click Next -> Name the Role IngestorRole -> Click Create role. 3. Create IAM Role for Transformer Lambda This function needs greater power to call AI and activate the Athena Data Catalog.
Repeat the Role creation steps from the section above (AWS service -> Lambda). In the search box, find and check 4 permissions: AmazonS3FullAccess AmazonBedrockFullAccess AmazonAthenaFullAccess AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole Click Next -> Name the Role TransformerRole -> Click Create role. Security Best Practice: In a production enterprise environment, we would not use *FullAccess permissions but instead write Inline Policies that limit access to a specific S3 Bucket. However, within the scope of this Data Pipeline practical exercise, using Managed Policies will help you avoid unnecessary “Access Denied” errors.

title: Create Lambda Reader API
content:
Lambda Reader is a standalone Lambda function distinct from Lambda QMJ Loader. It receives ticker requests from API Gateway and queries DynamoDB.
Step Action Technical Details 1 AWS Lambda → Functions → create function Select Author from scratch 2 Function name Enter stock-screener-reader 3 Runtime Select a supported Python runtime in the Console 4 Execution role select Use an existing role → LambdaStockScreenerReaderRole 5 Select Create function Open the Code tab 6 Paste the source code below This function does not read S3 and does not execute awswrangler 7 Configuration → Environment variables Add environment variable DYNAMODB_TABLE=qmj_screener 8 Select Deploy Save code Lambda source code import json import os from decimal import Decimal import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key TABLE_NAME = os.environ["DYNAMODB_TABLE"] table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(TABLE_NAME) def json_default(value): # DynamoDB returns Decimal; API response requires JSON number. if isinstance(value, Decimal): return float(value) raise TypeError(f"Unsupported type: {type(value)}") def response(status_code, body): return { "statusCode": status_code, "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET,OPTIONS", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type" }, "body": json.dumps(body, default=json_default) } def lambda_handler(event, context): params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {} ticker = (params.get("ticker") or "").strip().upper() if not ticker: return response(400, {"message": "ticker is required"}) result = table.query( KeyConditionExpression=Key("ticker").eq(ticker), ScanIndexForward=True ) return response(200, { "ticker": ticker, "items": result.get("Items", []) })

content:
This is the soul of the system. We will create an ETL Job on AWS Glue to read JSON files, flatten the player array, and write output as Parquet.
Step Action Technical Details 1 Open AWS Glue In the Console, find AWS Glue > Select ETL jobs (left menu). 2 Initialize Job Select the Script editor option > Select Spark > Click Create script. 3 Configure Job Details Switch to the Job details tab. Set name: dota2_etl_job. Under IAM Role, select Glue_Dota2_Processing_Role (created in Step 2.2). 4 Optimize cost In the Job bookmark section, select Enable. In the Number of workers section, reduce from 10 to 2 (Since we are using a small dataset, we don’t need large machines). 5 Insert Code Switch back to the Script tab, paste the PySpark code below. Remember to replace the RAW_PATH and PROCESSED_PATH variables with your Bucket names. 6 Save and Run Click Save > Click Run. Wait about 2-3 minutes, then check the S3 Processed Bucket to see the results. Complete PySpark code:
import sys from awsglue.transforms import * from awsglue.utils import getResolvedOptions from pyspark.context import SparkContext from awsglue.context import GlueContext from awsglue.job import Job from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, col, from_unixtime, to_date sc = SparkContext.getOrCreate() glueContext = GlueContext(sc) spark = glueContext.spark_session RAW_PATH = "s3://dota2-raw-zone-yourname/raw_matches/" PROCESSED_PATH = "s3://dota2-processed-zone-yourname/matches_parquet/" # 1. Read raw JSON data print("Starting to read data from S3 Raw...") df = spark.read.json(RAW_PATH) # 2. Process data (Flattening) # Explode the participants array into individual rows df_exploded = df.select( col("match_id"), to_date(from_unixtime(col("start_time"))).alias("match_date"), explode(col("players")).alias("player") ) # Extract required fields from the player object df_final = df_exploded.select( "match_id", "match_date", col("player.account_id").alias("account_id"), col("player.hero_id").alias("hero_id"), col("player.win").alias("is_win") ) # 3. Write data in Snappy-compressed Parquet format print("Starting to write data in Parquet format...") df_final.write.mode("append") \ .partitionBy("match_date") \ .parquet(PROCESSED_PATH, compression="snappy") print("ETL Job complete!")

import requests import boto3 import json from datetime import datetime # API and S3 configuration API_URL = "https://api.opendota.com/api/proMatches" BUCKET_NAME = "dota2-raw-zone-yourname" # Replace with your S3 Raw Bucket name PREFIX = "raw_matches" def fetch_and_upload(): print("Calling OpenDota API...") response = requests.get(API_URL) if response.status_code == 200: matches = response.json() # Create path following Apache Hive Partitioning standard (dt=YYYY-MM-DD) date_str = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d") file_name = f"matches_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}.json" s3_key = f"{PREFIX}/dt={date_str}/{file_name}" # PutObject to Amazon S3 s3 = boto3.client('s3') s3.put_object( Bucket=BUCKET_NAME, Key=s3_key, Body=json.dumps(matches), ContentType='application/json' ) print(f"Success! Pushed {len(matches)} matches to S3 at: {s3_key}") else: print("API error:", response.status_code) if __name__ == "__main__": fetch_and_upload()

title: Upgrade Glue Job: Calculate & Load Metrics
content:
We proceed to upgrade the PySpark source code of the AWS Glue Job. In addition to saving Parquet files to S3, Glue will directly calculate the Winrate and Pickrate, and use the boto3 library to push the results directly into DynamoDB.
Step Action Technical Details 1 Open Glue Studio In the AWS Console > Find AWS Glue > Under ETL Jobs > Open the source code of the dota2_etl_job created in section 2.3. 2 Update Script Select the Script tab, clear the old code, and replace it with the upgraded PySpark code below. 3 Configure Parameters Ensure the RAW_PATH, PROCESSED_PATH, and DynamoDB table name variables match your system. 4 Save and Run Click Save > Click Run to launch the aggregated metrics pipeline. 5 Verify Results Go to DynamoDB Console > Under Tables > Click the dota2_hero_metrics table > Click Explore table items to verify that Hero metrics records have been successfully loaded. Upgraded PySpark Source Code (dota2_etl_job_v2.py):
import sys import boto3 from pyspark.context import SparkContext from awsglue.context import GlueContext from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, col, from_unixtime, to_date, count, sum as _sum, when, lit sc = SparkContext.getOrCreate() glueContext = GlueContext(sc) spark = glueContext.spark_session RAW_PATH = "s3://dota2-raw-zone-yourname/raw_matches/" PROCESSED_PATH = "s3://dota2-processed-zone-yourname/matches_parquet/" DYNAMODB_TABLE = "dota2_hero_metrics" # 1. Read raw data and flatten df = spark.read.json(RAW_PATH) df_exploded = df.select( col("match_id"), to_date(from_unixtime(col("start_time"))).alias("match_date"), explode(col("players")).alias("player") ) df_final = df_exploded.select( "match_id", "match_date", col("player.hero_id").alias("hero_id"), col("player.win").alias("is_win") ) # [Chapter 2 Optimization]: Write clean long-term data as Snappy Parquet to S3 df_final.write.mode("append").partitionBy("match_date").parquet(PROCESSED_PATH, compression="snappy") # 2. [Chapter 4 Upgrade]: Calculate Aggregation Metrics using Spark DataFrame API print("Calculating aggregated Winrate and Pickrate for Heroes...") total_matches = df.count() df_metrics = df_final.groupBy("hero_id").agg( count("match_id").alias("total_picks"), _sum(when(col("is_win") == True, 1).otherwise(0)).alias("total_wins") ) # Calculate percentage metrics df_metrics = df_metrics.withColumn("win_rate", (col("total_wins") / col("total_picks")) * 100) \ .withColumn("pick_rate", (col("total_picks") / lit(total_matches)) * 100) # 3. Push data to DynamoDB using boto3 with Spark distributed partitions def upload_row_to_dynamodb(row): # Initialize boto3 client inside each Spark Cluster Worker Node dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='ap-southeast-1') table = dynamodb.Table(DYNAMODB_TABLE) # Perform Upsert action (Insert new or update existing hero_id) table.put_item( Item={ 'hero_id': int(row['hero_id']), 'total_picks': int(row['total_picks']), 'total_wins': int(row['total_wins']), 'win_rate': str(round(row['win_rate'], 2)), # Cast to string to avoid Float format issues in DynamoDB 'pick_rate': str(round(row['pick_rate'], 2)) } ) # Execute distributed operation across all DataFrame rows print("Starting distributed data load into Amazon DynamoDB...") df_metrics.rdd.foreach(upload_row_to_dynamodb) print("Data load complete!")

title: Building an AI-Driven Serverless Data Lakehouse for Clickstream
content:
Problem Statement In the digital age, understanding user (reader) behavior in real time is the key to survival for electronic newspaper platforms. Processing massive clickstream data (unstructured JSON) requires a fully automated system from data ingestion, compression, and transformation (ETL) to feeding it into an AI model for personalized article recommendations, while optimizing operational costs close to $0.
Serverless Architecture (Event-Driven) The system is designed following the Event-Driven Architecture and Zero-ETL architecture with 3 main processing layers:
Ingestion Layer: Collects real-time clickstream data from an emulator and automatically compresses it on-the-fly from JSON to columnar format (Parquet). Orchestration & ETL Layer: Orchestrates the entire workflow, completely resolving “Race Condition” errors between services, and invokes Serverless SQL to transform data into standard formats for AI. Storage & AI Layer: Stores massive amounts of data on a Data Lake and trains an Artificial Intelligence model (Recommender System) with a strict cost management strategy. Technology Highlights Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose: A gateway that receives streaming data and directly converts JSON to Parquet based on the AWS Glue Schema. AWS Step Functions: The “conductor” that orchestrates the entire workflow, perfectly handling Data Latency and Race Condition issues using Wait States. AWS Lambda & Amazon Athena: Handles Serverless ETL logic to transform data extremely fast without maintaining servers. Amazon S3: Physical storage repository (Data Lake) containing Parquet and CSV files. Amazon Personalize: Automated machine learning model (AutoML) for recommending articles, combined with an ultra-saving FinOps “Hit and Run” strategy. title: Data Ingestion Layer with AWS SQS & Lambda
content:
Welcome to the first critical stage: Building the Data Collection Pipeline. Instead of a bulky monolithic design, we will build a Decoupled architecture using Amazon SQS as a buffer between “finding videos” and “scraping comments”.
Goals of this stage: Create a queue using AWS SQS. Write the Producer_Lambda function to find top trending videos and push IDs to the queue. Write the Ingestor_Lambda function to read IDs from the queue, deep-paginate comments, and save to the S3 Data Lake. Step 1: Create State Database (Amazon DynamoDB) We need 2 notebooks so the Lambda system does not “lose memory” after each run.
Access the DynamoDB service on AWS Console.
Click Create table to create the first table (Comment tracking notebook):
Table name: YoutubeCommentsTracker Partition key: comment_id (Data type: String) Click Create table. Continue clicking Create table to create the second table (Error video blacklist):
Table name: YoutubeVideoBlacklist Partition key: video_id (Data type: String) Click Create table. Step 2: Create the Amazon SQS Queue SQS (Simple Queue Service) acts as a shock absorber. If YouTube returns too many videos, SQS will hold them back so the system can process them gradually, preventing overload.
Access Amazon SQS on the AWS Console.
Select Create queue.
Choose type Standard.
Name it: YoutubeVideoQueue. Keep the default settings and click Create queue. Note: Copy the Queue URL for use in the next step. Step 3: Build Producer Lambda This function searches for videos based on a keyword list. To optimize cost and avoid exhausting the API Quota, we limit to 3 top videos per keyword and check against the “Blacklist” before sending.
Access AWS Lambda, create a new function named Producer_Lambda (Python 3.x).
Attach the IngestorRole created in part 2 (it already has access to DynamoDB and SQS, so no new role is needed). Set the timeout to give Producer enough running time. Add Environment Variable: YOUTUBE_API_KEY.
Paste the following code and click Deploy: import json import boto3 import urllib.request import urllib.parse import os sqs = boto3.client('sqs') dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') blacklist_table = dynamodb.Table('YoutubeVideoBlacklist') # Replace with your Queue URL from Step 2 QUEUE_URL = 'https://sqs.<region>.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/YoutubeVideoQueue' def get_video_ids_by_keyword(api_key, query, max_results=3): encoded_query = urllib.parse.quote(query) url = f"https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/search?part=snippet&type=video&q={encoded_query}&key={api_key}&maxResults={max_results}" try: req = urllib.request.Request(url) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: data = json.loads(response.read().decode('utf-8')) return [item['id']['videoId'] for item in data.get('items', []) if item['id'].get('videoId')] except Exception as e: print(f"Search error: {e}") return [] def lambda_handler(event, context): API_KEY = os.environ.get('YOUTUBE_API_KEY') keywords = ["review iphone 16", "review electric car", "review laptop 2026", "review RE9"] all_video_ids = [] # Fetch 3 videos per keyword (total 12 videos) for kw in keywords: ids = get_video_ids_by_keyword(API_KEY, kw) all_video_ids.extend(ids) unique_video_ids = list(set(all_video_ids)) pushed_count = 0 for vid in unique_video_ids: # Check Blacklist to skip videos that previously errored (e.g., comments disabled) db_response = blacklist_table.get_item(Key={'video_id': vid}) if 'Item' in db_response: continue sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL, MessageBody=json.dumps({"video_id": vid})) pushed_count += 1 return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': f"Scanned and pushed {pushed_count} videos safely to SQS."} Step 4: Build Ingestor Lambda This function is automatically triggered (Triggered) every time a message arrives in SQS. It uses Pagination to deep-dig comments, while cross-checking with DynamoDB to ensure duplicate data is never collected.
Create a new Lambda function: Ingestor_Lambda.
In the Add trigger section, select source SQS, pointing to the YoutubeVideoQueue just created. Set the timeout to give Ingestor enough running time. Paste the optimized scraping code below:
import json import boto3 import urllib.request import os from datetime import datetime s3 = boto3.client('s3') dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') tracker_table = dynamodb.Table('YoutubeCommentsTracker') blacklist_table = dynamodb.Table('YoutubeVideoBlacklist') BUCKET_NAME = 'your-datalake-bucket-name' # Replace with your Bucket name def get_comments_for_video(api_key, video_id, target_new_comments=50, max_pages=10): new_items = [] next_page_token = "" pages_searched = 0 # Loop deep until 50 new comments are found OR all pages are exhausted while len(new_items) < target_new_comments and pages_searched < max_pages: url = f"https://www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/commentThreads?part=snippet&videoId={video_id}&key={api_key}&maxResults=50" if next_page_token: url += f"&pageToken={next_page_token}" try: req = urllib.request.Request(url) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: data = json.loads(response.read().decode('utf-8')) items = data.get('items', []) if not items: break for item in items: if len(new_items) >= target_new_comments: break comment_id = item['id'] db_response = tracker_table.get_item(Key={'comment_id': comment_id}) # Only process if comment has never existed in Tracker if 'Item' not in db_response: snippet = item['snippet']['topLevelComment']['snippet'] new_items.append({ 'id': comment_id, 'authorDisplayName': snippet.get('authorDisplayName', 'Unknown'), 'textOriginal': snippet.get('textOriginal', ''), 'publishedAt': snippet.get('publishedAt', '') }) # Mark as scraped in DB tracker_table.put_item(Item={'comment_id': comment_id, 'video_id': video_id}) next_page_token = data.get('nextPageToken') pages_searched += 1 if not next_page_token: break except Exception as e: if pages_searched == 0: blacklist_table.put_item(Item={'video_id': video_id, 'reason': str(e)}) break return {"video_id": video_id, "items": new_items} def lambda_handler(event, context): API_KEY = os.environ.get('YOUTUBE_API_KEY') for record in event['Records']: body = json.loads(record['body']) vid = body['video_id'] payload = get_comments_for_video(API_KEY, vid) # Only save S3 file if there is actually NEW data if len(payload['items']) > 0: now = datetime.now() file_name = f"comments_{vid}_{int(now.timestamp())}.json" s3_key = f"raw_data/year={now.year}/month={now.strftime('%m')}/day={now.strftime('%d')}/{file_name}" s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET_NAME, Key=s3_key, Body=json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False)) return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': "Consumer processing complete."} Step 5: Configure Test Event and Run System Test To trigger the system for the first time, we need to create a seed event (Test Event) for the Producer function. Since this function already has a keyword list in the code, this Test Event is purely procedural.
Open the Producer_Lambda function on the AWS Console. Click the small arrow next to the blue Test button (or select the Test tab). Select Configure test event. Fill in the following: Event name: TestProducer Event JSON: You can keep the default AWS code, or clear it and leave an empty brace {}. Click Save. Now, take a deep breath and click the blue Test button! Results Within a few minutes, the system will automatically scan, push to the queue, deep-dig data and save neatly to the raw_data/ folder in the S3 Data Lake. This architecture ensures the system never re-scrapes old data, optimizing all AWS resource costs.

title: Building a Serverless Data Lakehouse: Dota 2 Meta Analytics
content:
Introduction: Dota 2 Meta Analytics Data Lakehouse Dota 2 is not only a billion-dollar eSports title with the world’s most prestigious tournament (The International), but behind it lies a massive Big Data goldmine. Every second, millions of movement decisions, skill usages, and item purchases by professional players are systematically recorded.
Problem Statement: How can we collect hundreds of thousands of complex JSON files from an API, clean them, and analyze which “Meta” (which Heroes or items currently have the highest win rate) to serve players for real-time lookup… without “burning through” server maintenance costs?
This project is the answer. It guides you step-by-step in building a 100% Serverless Data Lakehouse on AWS. By rigorously applying FinOps (cloud cost optimization) and Decoupling (architecture separation) principles, this system can process massive amounts of data at a cost approaching… zero!
System Architecture This project is designed to Enterprise architecture standards, clearly divided into 4 independent layers (Swimlanes). This separation ensures that if one layer fails (e.g., the API goes down), the other layers continue to operate normally (Fault Tolerance).
Data Flow Details: 1. Ingestion & Automation Layer
Action: Uses AWS Lambda (triggered daily via EventBridge Cron) to call the OpenDota API. Result: Fetches professional match data in JSON format and ingests directly into Amazon S3 (Raw Zone). Data is partitioned by the standard dt=YYYY-MM-DD from the start. 2. Processing / ETL Layer
Action: S3 Event Notifications automatically trigger AWS Glue (PySpark) jobs upon new file arrival. Result: Glue jobs parse JSON, flatten 10-player data arrays into tabular schemas, and output Snappy-compressed Parquet files to Amazon S3 (Processed Zone). 3. Analytics Layer
Action: Configures Amazon Athena for data engineers to run ad-hoc SQL queries on S3 Processed data. Optimization: Implements Partition Projection in Athena instead of Glue Crawlers, accelerating query execution and minimizing scanning costs. 4. Serving & API Layer
Action: AWS Glue calculates aggregated metrics (Winrate, Pickrate) and upserts them directly into Amazon DynamoDB. Serving the UI: When a user accesses a static Web page (hosted on S3 Static Hosting), the Web calls HTTP API Gateway → Lambda Backend → Reads DynamoDB and returns results (latency below 100ms). FinOps Strategy: Static data such as hero images, item names, and skill descriptions are not stored in the Data Lake to reduce costs. The Frontend fetches them directly from the game’s library API (Direct Fetch). What Will You Learn From This Project? Upon completing this series, you will master the practical skills of a Modern Data Engineer:
Serverless Orchestration: Connect Lambda, S3, Glue, and EventBridge into a fully automated pipeline without managing a single server. PySpark ETL: Perform complex data transformations (Flattening Arrays) and apply the Parquet compression standard. Advanced Athena: Master the Partition Projection technique. Cloud Security & FinOps: Apply Least Privilege IAM Roles and cost optimization strategies (Pay-per-request DynamoDB, Parquet Snappy Compression). title: Data Processing & LLM Integration with Amazon Bedrock (Transformation Layer)
content:
At the Transformation layer, raw JSON data from S3 will be analyzed, summarized, and automatically sentiment-labeled. The system uses an Event-Driven architecture with an S3 Trigger to activate the Transformer_Lambda function. Natural language processing (NLP) is handled by the Claude 4.5 Haiku model via Amazon Bedrock.
Goals of this stage: Configure LLM model access on Amazon Bedrock. Set up the data processing Lambda function and S3 Event Trigger. Deploy source code optimized for token cost and JSON error handling (Data Chunking & Error Handling). Step 1: Enable the LLM Model on Amazon Bedrock Although the project infrastructure is in Asia, the AI processing flow will use Cross-Region Inference to the US East (N. Virginia) region to leverage the latest model generations and best quotas.
Switch Region on the AWS Console to US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1. Access the Amazon Bedrock service -> Select Model catalog. Scroll down and find Claude haiku 4.5 and click on it. Scroll down and find the Model ID section and copy that ID (will be used in Step 3). Step 2: Initialize Transformer Lambda and S3 Trigger This function acts as a Controller, routing data from S3 to Bedrock and writing results back to S3.
Access AWS Lambda, create a new function: Transformer_Lambda (Python 3.12), using the TransformerRole created in section 2. Configure Timeout: Access the Configuration tab -> General configuration -> Set Timeout to 15 minutes (ensures sufficient time to process large JSON files). In the Code tab, select + Add trigger to configure the event flow:
Source: S3 Bucket: Select the Data Lake Bucket. Event types: All object create events Prefix: raw_data/ (Required to prevent Infinite Loop) Suffix: .json Click Add. Step 3: Deploy Transformation Source Code The code below solves 3 major challenges when working with LLMs in a Production environment:
Cost Optimization: Limit output tokens by asking AI to return a summary (10-15 words) instead of a full translation. Data Chunking: Split the comment list into small batches (15 items/batch) to avoid exceeding Bedrock’s max_tokens. JSON Parsing Fallback: Build a 3-layer filter to safely catch and handle truncated JSON strings generated by AI errors. Deploy the following code into the Transformer_Lambda function and click Deploy:
import json import boto3 import urllib.parse import time s3 = boto3.client('s3') # Explicitly specify us-east-1 Region to use Inference Profile bedrock = boto3.client('bedrock-runtime', region_name='us-east-1') def analyze_sentiment_batch(comments): prompt = f"""You are a data analysis expert. Read the following YouTube comments and perform: 1. Identify the original language. 2. Evaluate sentiment (POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, NEUTRAL). 3. Summarize the main point in English (maximum 15 words). Ignore slang and symbols. RETURN ONLY 1 VALID JSON ARRAY. NO MARKDOWN. Required structure: "id", "language", "vietnamese_summary", "sentiment". Input data: {json.dumps(comments, ensure_ascii=False)} """ body = json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 4000, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], "temperature": 0 }) try: response = bedrock.invoke_model( modelId='us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0', body=body ) response_body = json.loads(response.get('body').read()) ai_response_text = response_body['content'][0]['text'].strip() # Safe JSON string parsing logic start_idx = ai_response_text.find('[') end_idx = ai_response_text.rfind(']') if start_idx != -1 and end_idx != -1 and end_idx > start_idx: clean_json = ai_response_text[start_idx:end_idx + 1] sentiment_results = json.loads(clean_json) return { item['id']: { 'sentiment': item.get('sentiment', 'UNKNOWN'), 'language': item.get('language', 'Unknown'), 'vietnamese_text': item.get('vietnamese_summary', 'No summary') } for item in sentiment_results } else: print(f"[ERROR] Invalid JSON response from LLM: {ai_response_text}") return {} except Exception as e: print(f"[ERROR] Bedrock Invocation Failed: {e}") return {} def chunk_list(lst, chunk_size): for i in range(0, len(lst), chunk_size): yield lst[i:i + chunk_size] def lambda_handler(event, context): for record in event['Records']: bucket_name = record['s3']['bucket']['name'] file_key = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(record['s3']['object']['key']) response = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket_name, Key=file_key) raw_data = json.loads(response['Body'].read().decode('utf-8')) all_comments = [{"id": item['id'], "text": item['textOriginal']} for item in raw_data.get('items', [])] if not all_comments: continue final_analysis_mapping = {} batch_size = 15 # Batch limit chunks = list(chunk_list(all_comments, batch_size)) for index, chunk in enumerate(chunks): mapping = analyze_sentiment_batch(chunk) final_analysis_mapping.update(mapping) if index < len(chunks) - 1: time.sleep(1) # Prevent Rate Limiting errors from Bedrock API processed_items = [] for item in raw_data.get('items', []): analysis = final_analysis_mapping.get(item['id'], {}) item['sentiment'] = analysis.get('sentiment', 'UNKNOWN') item['language'] = analysis.get('language', 'Unknown') item['vietnamese_text'] = analysis.get('vietnamese_text', 'Translation error') processed_items.append(item) raw_data['items'] = processed_items # Move data to processed_data partition path_parts = file_key.split('/') path_parts[0] = 'processed_data' new_file_key = '/'.join(path_parts) s3.put_object(Bucket=bucket_name, Key=new_file_key, Body=json.dumps(raw_data, ensure_ascii=False)) print(f"[SUCCESS] Processed data saved to: {new_file_key}") return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': "Transformation Completed."} Step 4: Pipeline Testing To verify the entire Ingestion and Transformation flow works synchronously:
Re-trigger the Producer_Lambda function from Chapter 3 by running the Test Event. Monitor the CloudWatch Logs of the Transformer_Lambda function to track batch processing progress. Access Amazon S3, check the processed_data/ folder. Download a JSON file and confirm that the vietnamese_text, language, and sentiment fields have been successfully labeled.
